explanation: `list(c)` calls `iter(c)`, i.e. `c.__iter__()`. Here `__iter__` contains `yield`, so every call creates a new, fresh generator: the object can be iterated as many times as you want. Only a single generator or iterator object gets exhausted.

stem: `x` and `y` are instances of a class that defines five methods: `__str__`, `__getitem__`, `__call__`, `__length__` and `__plus__` (each one records its name when it is called). Which statements are true? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: Python maps syntax to fixed special-method names: `print`/`str()` → `__str__`, `[]` → `__getitem__`, `()` → `__call__`, `len()` → `__len__`, `+` → `__add__`. Names such as `__length__` or `__plus__` are not special: defining them changes nothing, and `len(x)` / `x + y` raise TypeError.

distractor_notes.d: The hook used by `len()` is `__len__`; `__length__` is just an ordinary method name.

distractor_notes.d: The list shows the text returned by `__repr__` as is; quotes appear only for elements that are themselves strings.

stem: Given the code, which expressions evaluate to True? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: `isinstance` and `issubclass` follow the parent chain upward: a Bass is a Guitar and an Instrument, and every class is a subclass of `object`. They never go downward (a Guitar is not a Bass) or sideways (Drum and Guitar are siblings). `isinstance(Guitar, Instrument)` asks whether the class object Guitar is an Instrument instance: it is not, it is a subclass.

distractor_notes.b: Inheritance goes upward only: a Guitar is not necessarily a Bass.
distractor_notes.c: Drum and Guitar are siblings, both children of Instrument.
distractor_notes.f: Guitar is a class, not an instance; `issubclass(Guitar, Instrument)` would be True.

distractor_notes.e: 3.0 is a float even though its value is a whole number.
